messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Malo, a 63-year-old construction worker from Honolulu, had spent nearly forty years on high beams and scaffolding, a man who trusted his hands and his balance. But for twenty-five of those years, when he came home, his wife Leilani would turn her anger on him—slaps across the face, a shove into the kitchen counter, once a lamp thrown at his back. He never fought back. He never told anyone. When she died of lung cancer six years ago, he expected relief. Instead, the memories burrowed deeper. The first time a co-worker clapped him on the shoulder and said “you okay?” Malo flinched so hard he nearly dropped his hammer; his heart hammered and he excused himself to stand by the door of the break room, scanning for exits before he could breathe again. That became a ritual: every room he entered, his eyes went first to the doors.

The triggers were specific and relentless. A woman at the grocery store with hands shaped like Leilani’s—pale, slender, with prominent knuckles—would freeze him mid-aisle. His chest would tighten, and he’d feel that old shame flood back, the thought *I’m weak* settling in his gut like a stone. He had come to believe he couldn’t rely on himself; if he couldn’t protect himself from one woman, how could he trust his own judgment about anything? When a neighbor mentioned his late wife in passing—“your Leilani used to love those plumeria”—Malo felt the ground drop out from under him. That night he couldn’t sleep, waking every hour to check the locks, the windows, the silence of the house. The smallest sound—a creak, the refrigerator humming—made him startle upright. He began sleeping with the bedroom door open so he could see the front door.

Over the months, Malo’s strategies took shape, each one seeming to make sense at the time but slowly tightening the trap. He started to avoid any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation, even at work. When a foreman asked if he could stay late, Malo just nodded, even though he needed to pick up his grandson; he couldn’t bring himself to say no, certain it would escalate into something he couldn’t handle. He found himself scanning every building for exits before he could settle his mind. But the scanning itself kept the image of Leilani’s angry face close, and every door he spotted became a fresh trigger — a reminder of the moment she had blocked the kitchen exit during one of her worst rages. And on payday, he began spending impulsively—a new watch he didn’t need, dinner at a restaurant he couldn’t afford, anything to drown the hollow feeling that he was dead inside. The spending gave him a brief lift, but afterward, looking at the credit card statement, he felt even more worthless, confirming his belief that he couldn’t trust himself with money or with anything else. The very act of avoiding conflict also boomeranged: by never talking about his past, he never processed it, so a stray comment or a pair of hands would catch him unprepared. His threat system was always scanning, always ready, which made him jump at ordinary sounds, and that hypervigilance itself seemed to summon reminders—he’d hear a door slam and instantly picture Leilani’s angry face, a trigger that solidified his sense of helplessness.

The chain coiled tighter. Because he believed he was weak, he avoided any potential friction at work, but that meant he accepted extra shifts he didn’t want, leading to exhaustion and more irritable nights. To calm down he’d go online and buy tools he didn’t need, then feel guilty and stop checking his bank account—another way his avoidance left him unmoored. One evening, a colleague mentioned his own wife’s new hobby, and Malo felt his throat close up. He left the site early, driving aimlessly, pulled into a hardware store, and bought a power saw he would never use. That night he lay awake, the saw still in its box on the floor, and thought, *I can’t rely on myself to even feel anything anymore.* The numbness scared him most.

What finally brought him to the clinic was a small crisis: his grandson, who had been staying with him on weekends, asked why Malo always sat with his back to the wall, watching the door. The boy didn’t know about Leilani. Malo realized he couldn’t let the next generation learn to live like this. He made an appointment at the VA’s community mental health center, though he drove past it twice before walking in. He is afraid—afraid that talking about it will break him open, that he truly is as weak as he fears. But he is also tired of spending money he doesn’t have, tired of being startled by a doorbell, tired of being a man who can’t sit in the middle of a room.
